column7: A quasar whose jet points almost straight at us: relativistic beaming makes the nucleus blaze, and the disk is seen face-on.
A near-maximally spinning black hole: the disk reaches in close to the horizon and the approaching side is strongly beamed. A stylized approximation of frame dragging, not full Kerr geodesics.

The 6.5 billion solar mass black hole in the galaxy Messier 87 as the Event Horizon Telescope imaged it: a bright ring, brighter on one side, with a long relativistic jet, seen about 17 degrees from the pole.
A stellar-mass black hole pulling a stream of gas off a blue supergiant companion into a small hot disk, with a faint jet. Modeled on Cygnus X-1.
The same quasar seen almost in the plane of the dusty torus: the torus hides the bright disk and the jets stand out to the sides, the way an obscured (type 2) active nucleus looks.
An active galactic nucleus seen from about 25 degrees off the pole: a very bright disk, a dusty torus around it and twin relativistic jets.

The 4.3 million solar mass black hole at the center of the Milky Way as the Event Horizon Telescope imaged it: a small, hot, faint flow with an orange crescent and a thin photon ring, seen about 30 degrees from the pole.

A hyperluminous quasar: a black hole of roughly 40 billion solar masses feeding an enormous, blazing disk with twin jets and a dusty torus. Its disk is drawn far larger than usual, in units of the horizon.
